RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Authorize a budget amendment for CIP Project # 205004  —

million in Fiscal Year 2025-26. 2. Authorize City Staff to develop and solicit a request for
proposals from qualified vendors to complete the scope of work outlined in the South Beach
Seawall Repair and Sand Restoration Project.

REPORT SUMMARY: Deteriorating infrastructure, exacerbated by sever storm conditions has
caused significant damage to the South Beach sea wall and groin wail. The conditions have
limited public access and contributed to the loss of the sandy beach area.

In 2016, the City began taking action to mitigate damage to the seawall; however, without a
substantial funding source, the City’s budget could not support a large scale project.

In 2022, the City developed the South Beach Seawall and Sand Restoration Project, the project
proposed to restore the seawall and groin wall as well as improve public access points and
replenish sand to combat ongoing erosion. The proposed enhancements will stabilize the beach,
protect nearby businesses and structures from storm damage, and increase recreational
opportunities for the community.

The City sought funding from a number of entities, and in April 2026 the Los Angeles County
Regional Park and Open Space District (RPOSD) awarded $2.48 million to support the South
Beach Seawall Repair and Sand Restoration Project.

With the project now funded through RPOSD, the City is ready to develop and solicit a request
for proposals from qualified vendors to complete the scope of work outlined in the South Beach
Seawall Repair and Sand Restoration Project.

In addition to requesting authorization to solicit a RFP, City Staff request the City Council
approve a budget amendment accounting for $2.48 million in grant funds from RPOSD and the
project budget for Fiscal Year 2025-26.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The South Beach
Seawall Repair and Sand Restoration Project will not begin.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implementation of City Council direction.
 FISCAL IMPACTS: Expenses associated with this project will be reimbursed by grant funds up
to $2.48 Million.

SUBJECT:  Authorization to Purchase Saltwater System Supplies for

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize the City Manager or their designee to purchase
saltwater system parts from Orange County Winwater Company utilizing Saltwater Fund
11325-6552 for an amount of not-to-exceed $80,000.

REPORT SUMMARY: The Public Works Department maintains and operates the City’s
saltwater systems, which requires a reliable inventory of repair parts to ensure timely
response to system failures, leaks, and ongoing maintenance needs. The saltwater
system is critical to supporting daily operations and ensuring uninterrupted utility service
for the community.

conducted an informal competitive procurement process and obtained three quotes for

and gate valves. These components are essential for emergency repairs, valve
replacements, pipeline maintenance, and system rehabilitation projects. The following
quotes were received:

funds are available in the FY 2025-2026 Saltwater Fund 11325-6552.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): (1): Authorize City Manager, or their designee, to procure
per the City’s purchasing policy, three (3) 2026 GEM E6 LSV carts for a not-to-exceed sum
of $160,000.00 from the lowest responsive bidder. (2). Amend the budget for the Avalon
Transit Fund to include a $160,000.00 expenditure for Vehicle Replacement Fund (Account
12325-6781) and $127,227 in offsetting grant revenues.

REPORT SUMMARY: At the June 2023 Metro Board meeting, $13,937,073 million of local
funds were approved for Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) and infrastructure projects for seven local
operators. This additional funding for ZEV projects helps to assist Local Transit Systems
Subcommittee (LTSS) members, which Avalon is a member of through Metro, in complying with
the California Air Resources Board (CARB) Innovative Clean Transit Rule (ICT), which requires
the phased-in purchase of ZEV.

The City of Avalon applied for and was awarded funding in the first round of ZEV Call for
Projects. With the award from the first round, the City purchased two (2) Ford E-Transit
vans for the City’s transportation program.

In early 2026 the City applied during the second Call for Projects to expand its GEM fleet
and was awarded $127,227 to purchase of three (3) GEM E6 vehicles. Per the terms of the
grant the City is required to contribute a minimum 20% match approximately $25,500.
  —

Since its implementation in April 2024, the City’s has experienced great success with its
micro transit program. Ridership has more than doubled with some months showing as
much as a 70% increase in ridership over pre-COVID users. Due to the demand, the City
has found it necessary to expand the fleet. The Polaris GEM E6 provides a versatile and
durable vehicle with proven success in providing high volume, mass transportation in other
Southern California cities. Manufactured in Anaheim. California, the vehicles are electric with
zero emissions and exceed Low Speed Vehicle federal manufacturing standards.

As required by the City’s procurement policy, City Staff solicited quotes from three (3)
Southern California GEM dealers for three (3) fully loaded Polaris GEM E6 vehicles. At the
time this report was authored, two dealers had provided quotes, the third did not provide a
responsive bid:

SUBJECT:  Appeal of Oversized Vehicle Permit

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Open the Public Hearing. 2. Receive Public Comment. 3.
Close the Public Hearing. 4. Consider applicant appeal and determine to: a.) Uphold the decision
of the Vehicle Hearing Officer, or b.) Overturn the decision of the Vehicle Hearing Officer, or c.)
Issue a Temporary Permit until Avalon Municipal Code §4-4 revision.

BACKGROUND: On March 25, 2026 Mr. John Warner submitted a Residential Vehicle Hearing
Application for an oversized transfer of a Residential Vehicle Permit (replacing a 2005 Nissan
Frontier approximately 205” in length with a 2018 Toyota Tacoma approximately 208” in length).
On April 17, 2026, the Vehicle Hearing Officer conducted a hearing on the application and on
April 23, 2026 subsequently denied the oversized Residential Vehicle Permit transfer due to the
fact the replacement vehicle is 3” greater in length. A copy of the decision letter is attached to
this report.

On May 4, 2026, Mr. John Warner submitted a request, and paid the applicable hearing fees, to
appeal the decision to deny the oversize Residential Vehicle permit which is attached to this
agenda report for Council consideration.
City Staff support the findings of the Vehicle Hearing Officer denying the permit are consistent
with AMC §4-4-1705.1 Replacement of Vehicles ‘The holder of a valid vehicle permit may
replace the vehicle with a vehicle in the same category, provided that the replacement vehicle
is within the size limits established by § 4-4.1705(a). An oversized vehicle that has been issued
an oversized vehicle permit may not be replaced by a larger vehicle. No exceptions to this
oversized vehicle rule may be made by the Vehicle Clerk, the Vehicle Hearing Officer, or any
other person.”

However, during the March 4, 2025 City Council Meeting Vehicle Ordinance discussion item,
Council discussed increasing the maximum length of a full-size vehicle from 200” to 210” in the
next ordinance revision. As such and alternatively, the City Council could approve staff issuing
a Temporary Vehicle Permit until ordinance revision returns to Council for adoption to occur later
this year.

John Warner (“Applicant”) submitted an application for a vehicle permit for an oversized

to 206 inches in length. Applicant seeks approval of a replacçrnent vehicle measuring

 CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

 The Hearing Officer has jurisdiction to hear and decide this matter pursuant to the Avalon
 Municipal Code. Section 4-4-1705.1 governs the approval of oversized vehicles and imposes
 a mandatory limitation on approval authority. Section 4-4-1705.1 prohibits approval of any
 oversized vehicle that exceeds the length of a previously approved oversized vehicle. The
express language of the Code provides that no exceptions may be made by the Hearing
Officer or any other person, thereby eliminating any discretion in the approval of a larger
replacement oversized vehicle. Even if the Applicant’s circumstances or intended uses are
reasonable or compelling, such equitable considerations cannot be considered where the
governing law expressly removes discretion. Because the proposed vehicle exceeds the
length of the previously approved oversized vehicle, the Hearing Officer lacks legal authority
to approve the application.

DECISION

The application of John Warner for a vehicle permit for an oversized vehicle is DENIED.

All property owners and customers of record whose parcels receive sewer, saltwater, and solid waste services
provided by the City of Avalon are being issued this public hearing notice. The proposed rate changes may apply
to all parcels that receive sewer, saltwater, and solid waste services from the City of Avalon. The hearing is open

Why Are Rate Changes Being Considered?
The City is committed to providing the highest quality utility services at the lowest possible rates for our
customers, maintaining financially sound and fiscally responsible sewer, saltwater, and solid waste programs,
all while keeping pace with inflation and other cost increases. To meet this commitment, the City engaged an
independent consultant to evaluate the infrastructure needs and operations and maintenance costs of its sewer,
saltwater, and solid waste utilities. This review assessed the adequacy of rate revenues to operate and maintain
the utilities and comply with all state and federal regulations. Based on this evaluation, it has been determined
that rate increases are necessary to enable the City to:

  •  Recover current and projected increases in the costs of operating and maintaining the sewer, saltwater,
  and solid waste systems;
  •  Construct capital infrastructure improvements needed to repair, replace and update City’s aging sewer
  and saltwater systems and expand the height of the existing landfill to extend its useful life;
  •  Comply with all state and federal regulatory requirements; and
  •  Maintain prudent reserves to ensure operational and financial stability.

1.3 Generally Accepted Rate Setting Principles
As a practical matter, utilities should consider setting rates on generally accepted or global
principles and guidelines. In summary form, utility rates should be:
  •  Cost-based, proportional, and set at a level that meets the utility’s full revenue
  requirement
  •  Easy to understand and administer
  •  Designed to conform with generally accepted rate setting techniques
  •  Stable in their ability to provide adequate revenues for meeting the utility’s financial,
  operating, and regulatory requirements
  •  Established at a level that is stable from year-to-year from a customer’s perspective
  •  Established in compliance with State and local legislative requirements

setting rates. This approach conforms to most public utility budgetary requirements and the
calculation is easily developed. A public utility:

  •  Adds operations and maintenance (O&M) expenses to applicable taxes or transfer
  payments to determine total operating expenses. Operations and maintenance expenses

4.1 Rate Design Criteria and Considerations
Prudent rate administration dictates that several criteria that are considered when setting utility
rates. Some of these rate design criteria are listed below:
  •  Rates which are easy to understand from the customer’s perspective
  •  Rates which are easy for the City to administer
  •  Consideration of the customer’s ability to pay
  -  Cost-based and proportional
  •  Continuity, overtime, of the rate making philosophy
  •  Policy considerations (encourage efficient use, economic development, etc.)
  •  Provide revenue stability from month to month and year to year
  •  Promote efficient allocation of the resource
  •  Proportional and non-discriminatory (cost-based)
  •  Meet the requirements of Proposition 218
Given the requirement and intent of Proposition 218, the last consideration, cost-based rates,
should be of paramount importance and provide the primary guidance to utilities on rate
structure and policy. However, it is important that the City provides its customers with a proper
price signal as to what their consumption is costing. This goal may be approached through rate
level and structure. When developing the proposed rate designs, all the above-listed criteria can
be taken into consideration. However, it should be noted that it is difficult, if not impossible, to
design a rate that meets all the goals and objectives listed above. For example, it may be difficult
to design a rate that takes into consideration the customer’s ability to pay, and one which is cost-
based. In designing rates, there are always trade-offs between the goals and objectives and a
delicate balance must always be struck.

The establishment of cost-based and proportional rates was of paramount importance in the
development of the City’s sewer Study. Meeting the requirements and documenting the steps
taken to develop cost-based and proportional rates has been in the forefront with the legal

  1.4 Determining the Revenue Requirement
Most public utilities use the cash basis1 approach for establishing their revenue requirement and
setting rates. This approach conforms to most public utility budgetary requirements and the
calculation is easy to understand and determine. A public utility:
  •  Totals its cash expenditures for a period of time to determine required revenues
  •  Adds operation and maintenance (O&M) expenses to applicable taxes or transfer
  payments to determine total operating expenses. Operation and maintenance expenses
  include the materials, electricity, labor, supplies, etc. needed to keep the utility
  functioning.
  Calculates capital costs by adding debt service payments (principal and interest) to capital
  improvements financed with rate revenues. In lieu of including capital improvements
  financed with rate revenues, a utility sometimes includes annual depreciation expense to
  stabilize annual revenue requirement.

Under the cash basis approach, the sum of the capital and operating expenses equals the utility’s
revenue requirement during any period of time (see Table 1 2).  -

  Table 1-2

  Cash Basis  Utility Basis (Accrual)

  +  O&M Expense  +  O&M Expense
  +  Taxes or Transfer Payments  +  Taxes or Transfer Payments
  +  Capital Improvements Financed with Rate  +  Depreciation Expense
  Revenues ( Depreciation Exp.)
  +  Debt service (Principal + Interest)  +  Return on Investment
  =  Total Revenue Requirement  =  Total Revenue Requirement

Note that the two portions of the capital expense component (debt service and capital
improvements financed from rates) are necessary under the cash basis approach because utilities
generally cannot finance all their capital facilities with long-term debt. An exception occurs if a
public utility provides service to a wholesale or contract customer. In this situation, a public utility
could use the utility basis approach (see Table 1 2) to earn a reasonable return on its investment.

A saltwater cost of service analysis determines the proportional distribution of the total revenue
requirement to the rate structure components. The previously developed revenue requirement
(Section 2) for FY 2026-27 (test year) was utilized in the development of the cost of service
analysis.

3.1 Objectives of a Cost of Service Analysis
There are two primary objectives in conducting a cost of service analysis:
  •  Allocate and proportionally distribute the City’s saltwater revenue requirement, and
  •  Derive the cost basis for subsequent rate designs by customer class of service
The objectives of the cost of service analysis are different from determining a revenue
requirement. As noted in the previous section, a revenue requirement analysis determines the
utility’s overall financial needs, while the cost of service analysis determines the proportional
manner to collect the calculated revenue requirement.

3.2 Development of the Saltwater Cost of Service
The saltwater cost of service analysis was reviewed with regards to cost basis and the
proportionality. Saltwater services are not metered by the City. Given this, an approach was
developed to review the estimated flows by customer type. The assumed flow generated by each
customer class and their related contribution to flows from saltwater use to flush toilets was
reviewed. Based on industry sewer flow information, as saltwater flow data is not available as it
is not widely used for these types of services, the flow assumptions for the different customer
classes were developed.

3.3 Consultant’s Conclusions
The City has an established rate for residential customers (per account), and commercial and
hotels (per toilet). Given the current flow assumptions, which reflect industry standard sewer
flow ratios, the current relationships were maintained. Given this, the City’s proposed saltwater
rates can be developed.

   Saltwater Rate Design
The final step of the City’s comprehensive saltwater rate study is the design of proposed rates to
collect the appropriate levels of revenues, based on the results of both the revenue requirement
and the cost of service analyses. In developing the City’s proposed saltwater rates, consideration
is given to the level of the rates as well as the structure of the rates. The level of rates reflects
the amount of revenues that should be collected while the structure of the rates is how it is
collected (i.e., component charges) from the customers.

The overall revenue level for the City’s has been established in the revenue requirement analysis
(Section 2) while the proportional distribution of costs has been developed in the cost of service
analysis (Section 3) which provides the revenue levels to be collected based on cost causation
and the cost basis for each rate component.

4.1 Rate Design Criteria and Considerations
Prudent rate administration dictates that several criteria that are considered when setting utility
rates. Some of these rate design criteria are listed below:
  •  Rates which are easy to understand from the customer’s perspective
  •  Rates which are easy for the City to administer
  •  Consideration of the customer’s ability to pay
  •  Cost-based and proportional
  •  Continuity, overtime, of the rate making philosophy
  •  Policy considerations (encourage efficient use, economic development, etc.)
  •  Provide revenue stability from month to month and year to year
  •  Promote efficient allocation of the resource
  •  Proportional and non-discriminatory (cost-based)
  •  Meet the requirements of Proposition 218
Given the requirement and intent of Proposition 218, the last consideration, cost-based rates,
should be of paramount importance and provide the primary guidance to utilities on rate
structure and policy. However, it is important that the City provides its customers with a proper
price signal as to what the service is costing. This goal may be approached through rate level and
structure. When developing the proposed rate designs, all the above-listed criteria can be taken
into consideration. However, it should be noted that it is difficult, if not impossible, to design a
rate that meets all the goals and objectives listed above. For example, it may be difficult to design
a rate that takes into consideration the customer’s ability to pay, and one which is cost-based. In
designing rates, there are always trade-offs between the goals and objectives and a delicate
balance must always be struck.

The establishment of cost-based and proportional rates was of paramount importance in the
development of the City’s saltwater rate study. Meeting the requirements and documenting the
steps taken to develop cost-based and proportional rates has been in the forefront with the legal
challenges in the State of California on utility rates. A focus has been given to meeting the
requirements of California Constitution article XIII D, section 6 (Article XIII D). A key component

  Saltwater Rate Design  16
F  City of Avalon —SaitwaterRate Study
 of Article XIII D is the development of rates which reflect the cost of providing service and are
proportionally distributed between the customer classes of service, and the customers within
each class. HDR would point out that there is no single methodology for proportionally assigning
costs to the customer classes. The Water Environment Federation Manual of Practice #27
provides methodologies which may be used to establish cost-based rates. Unfortunately, Article
XIII D is not prescriptive and does not provide a specific methodologyfor establishing cost-based
rates.

HDR is of the opinion that the proposed rates meet the legal requirements of Article XIII D. HDR
reaches this conclusion based upon the following:
  •  The revenue derived from saltwater rates does not exceed the funds required to
  provide the property related service (i.e., saltwater service). The proposed rates are
  designed to collect the overall revenue requirement of the City’s saltwater system.
  •  The revenues derived from saltwater rates shall not be used for any purpose other than
  that for which the fee or charge is imposed. The revenues derived from the City’s
  saltwater rates are used exclusively to fund the City’s saltwater system O&M and provide
  adequate funding for capital improvement, repair, and replacement.
  •  The amount of a fee or charge imposed upon a parcel or person as an incident of
  property ownership shall not exceed the proportional costs of the service attributable
  to the parcel. The Study has appropriately grouped customers into customer classes of
  service (residential, etc.) that reflect the customer usage patterns and system
  requirements (i.e., the benefits they receive from and burdens they place on the system)
  of each customer class of service. The grouping of customers and rates into these classes
  of service creates the proportionality expected under Article XIII D by having differing
  rates by customer classes of service which reflect both the level of revenue to be collected
  by the utility, and the manner in which these costs are incurred and assigned to customer
  classes of service based upon their proportional impacts.

1.4 Determining the Revenue Requirement
Most public utilities use the cash basis1 approach for establishing the revenue requirement and
setting rates. This approach conforms to most public utility budgetary requirements and the
calculation is easy to understand and determine. A public utility:
  •  Totals its cash expenditures for a period of time to determine required revenues
  •  Adds operation and maintenance (O&M) expenses to applicable taxes or transfer
  payments to determine total operating expenses. Operation and maintenance expenses
  include the materials, electricity, labor, supplies, etc. needed to keep the utility
  functioning.
  •  Calculates capital costs by adding debt service payments (principal and interest) to
  capital improvements financed with rate revenues. In lieu of including capital
  improvements financed with rate revenues, a utility sometimes includes depreciation
  expense to stabilize annual revenue requirement.
Under the cash basis approach, the sum of the capital and operating expenses equals the utility’s
revenue requirement during any period of time (see Table 1 2).  -

   Solid Waste Cost of Service
In the previous section, the revenue requirement analysis focused on the total revenues required
to adequately fund the City’s solid waste utility. This section will provide an overview of the
second step in a comprehensive solid waste rate study; the cost of service analysis developed for
the City’s solid waste utility.

The objective of the cost of service analysis is different from determining the revenue
requirement. Whereas the revenue requirement analysis determines the utility’s overall revenue
needs, the cost of service analysis determines the proportional distribution of the revenue
requirement to establish proposed rates for the proposed time period. In this case, the revenue
requirement for FY 2026-27, the first year of the proposed rate transition plan, was used for
establishing the cost of service analysis.

3.1 Objectives of a Cost of Service Analysis
There are two primary objectives in conducting a cost of service analysis:
  •  Proportionally distribute the City’s solid waste revenue requirement, and
  •  Derive the cost basis for subsequent rate designs by customer class of service
The objectives of the cost of service analysis are different from determining a revenue
requirement. As noted in the previous section, a revenue requirement analysis determines the
utility’s overall financial needs, while the cost of service analysis determines the proportional
manner to collect the calculated revenue requirement.

3.2 Development of the Solid Waste Cost of Service
It is important to note, the City contracts for solid waste collection and disposal services.
Consequently, the City does not have information available on customers in regards to the size
of the solid waste container, the frequency of service for each customers, or the number of pick
ups. Given this, the information necessary to identify the cost components related to providing
service to the City’s customers is unavailable. It should also be noted that information on actual
waste generation by customer type is limited, as most collection and disposal practices do not
separate by customer type in a similar way to how the City charges for solid waste service. For
example, a utility typically does not have information on the average tonnage collected from an
individual restaurant or grocery store. At best, some utilities may have total tonnage collected by
residential or commercial in aggregate.

The City’s solid waste rate structure is further complicated by the fact that a customer may not
have a specified, or individual, solid waste disposal container. In many cases, multiple customers
dispose of their waste in a single solid waste disposal container. As such, the solid waste
contractor may collect waste multiple times a week, or even multiple times a day depending on
the need and activities in the area. Given this, it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine those
customers that benefit from a specific container or need at the current time. As a result, the
current rate structure relationships were maintained.

   4 Solid Waste Rate Design
The final step of the City’s comprehensive solid waste rate study is the design of proposed rates
to collect the appropriate levels of revenues, based on the results of both the revenue
requirement and the cost of service analyses. In developing the City’s proposed solid waste rates,
consideration is given to the level of the rates as well as the structure of the rates. The level of
rates reflects the amount of revenues that should be collected while the structure of the rates is
how it is collected (i.e., component charges) from the customers.

4.1 Rate Design Criteria and Considerations
Prudent rate administration dictates that several criteria should be considered when setting
utility rates. Some of these rate design criteria are listed below:
  •  Rates which are easy to understand from the customer’s perspective
  •  Rates which are easy for the City to administer
  •  Consideration of the customer’s ability to pay
  •  Cost-based
  •  Continuity, overtime, of the rate making philosophy
  •  Policy considerations
  •  Provide revenue stability from month to month and year to year
  •  Proportional and non-discriminatory (cost-based)
  •  Defensible (Proposition 218 compliant)
Given the requirement and intent of Proposition 218, the last consideration, cost-based rates,
should be of paramount importance and provide the primary guidance to utilities on rate
structure and policy. However, it is important that the City provides its customers with a proper
price signal as to what their consumption is costing. This goal may be approached through rate
level and structure. When developing the proposed rate designs, all the above-listed criteria can
be taken into consideration. However, it should be noted that it is difficult, if not impossible, to
design a rate that meets all the goals and objectives listed above. For example, it may be difficult
to design a rate that takes into consideration the customer’s ability to pay, and one which is cost-
based. In designing rates, there are always trade-offs between the goals and objectives and a
delicate balance must always be struck.

The establishment of cost-based and proportional solid waste rates was of paramount
importance in the development of the City’s Study. Meeting the requirements and documenting
the steps taken to develop cost-based and proportional rates has been in the forefront with the
legal challenges in the State of California on utility rates. A focus has been given to meeting the
requirements of California Constitution article XIII D, section 6 (Article XIII D). A key component
of Article XIII D is the development of rates which reflect the cost of providing service
and are proportionally distributed between the customer classes of service, and the customers
within each class. HDR would point out that there is no single methodology for proportionally
assigning costs to the customer classes. Unfortunately, Article XIII D is not prescriptive and does
not provide a specific methodology for establishing cost-based rates.

SUBJECT:  First Reading of an Ordinance Prohibiting Fireworks in the City of
  Avalon

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Introduce and waive all further readings of an ordinance
prohibiting the use, possession, sale and discharge of fireworks within the City of Avalon.

REPORT SUMMARY: Every year City of Avalon, LA County Fire and Sherriff personnel have
problems with illegal fireworks. Though the City has already adopted the Los Angeles County
Fire Code  —  which prohibits fireworks —  in order to simplify enforcement, staff recommends
adoption of a basic ordinance that prohibits the use, possession, sale and discharge of fireworks
within the city.

The intent of the new ordinance is to reasonably regulate the possession, sale, use or discharge
of dangerous fireworks within the city to protect the public health, safety, property and general
welfare of its residents and visitors alike. Avalon is located in a “Very High Fire Severity Zone.”
Illegal discharge of fireworks can easily lead to a large-scale fire within the City.

The ordinance makes it unlawful for any person or responsible party to possess, sell, use or
discharge dangerous fireworks unless a permit authorizing such possession, sale, use or
discharge has been issued by the Fire Chief to the person or responsible party using, selling, or
discharging or found in possession of said fireworks, and unless such person is in possession
of a valid pyrotechnic operator’s license issued by the Office of the State Fire Marshal. The Fire
Chief may establish reasonable rules and regulations for governing issuance of a firework permit
and may issue the same subject to payment of a fee as established by the City Council.

In addition to prohibiting fireworks in Avalon, the proposed ordinance establishes penalties from
$250 to $1,000 for each violation of the ordinance.

Additionally, if fireworks cause a fire or emergency response the person responsible will be held
financially responsible for the cost of fire suppression, emergency medical services, law
enforcement response, evacuation, and any related damages to the extent permitted by law.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Increased risk of
wildland and structure fires, serious injuries or fatalities to residents, visitors, pets and
emergency responders, Property damage to homes, businesses, vehicles, docks, and
surrounding natural areas.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implementation of City Council direction.
 FISCAL IMPACTS: Undetermined.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: Pursuant to the Brown Act.

  AN ORDINANCE OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF AVALON
  PROHIBITING THE USE, POSSESSION, SALE, AND DISCHARGE OF

  4-16.01 Purpose and Findings
  —

  The use, possession, sale, and discharge of fireworks within the City of Avalon
  pose a significant threat to public health, safety, and welfare due to the City’s
  unique island environment, wildfire risk, limited emergency access, and dense
  residential and visitor populations.

  Prohibiting fireworks is necessary to reduce the risk of fires, injuries, and disturb

 4-16.02 Definition
  —

As used in this Chapter ‘fireworks” means and includes:
  (1) Any combustible or explosive composition or any substance or combi
  nation of substances or articles prepared for the purpose of producing a
  visible or an audible effect by combustion, explosion, deflagration or det
  onation, whether manufactured, homemade or improvised;
  (2) Fireworks classified by the State Fire Marshal as “dangerous fireworks”
  and as “safe and sane fireworks” pursuant to Health and Safety Code Sec
  tions 12561 and 12562;
  (3) Any pyrotechnic devices for which the State Fire Marshal requires a
  license to manufacture, sell, transport or operate; and
  (4) Firecrackers, torpedoes, skyrockets, roman candles, cherry bombs,
  sparklers, chasers, snakes or other fireworks of like or similar construction
  and any fireworks containing any explosive or flammable compound or
  substance.

4-16.03 Fireworks Prohibited
  —

It shall be unlawful for any person to use, give, possess, sell, offer for sale, store,
ignite, discharge, or otherwise cause to explode any fireworks within the City of
Avalon unless a permit authorizing such possession, sale, use or discharge has
been issued by the Fire Chief to the person or responsible party using, selling, or
discharging or found in possession of said fireworks, and unless such person is in
possession of a valid pyrotechnic operator’s license issued by the Office of the
State Fire Marshal.
4-16.04 Penalties
  —

Whenever a peace officer charged with the enforcement of any provision of the
Municipal Code determines that a violation of this chapter has occurred, the
peace officer shall have the authority to issue an administrative citation to any
person responsible for the violation.
Whenever a peace officer charged with the enforcement of this chapter deter
mines that a violation of the chapter has occurred, the peace officer may issue an
administrative citation for each violation found to have occurred.
Citations issued pursuant to this chapter shall carry administrative fines as fol
lows:
  $250 for the first and subsequent violations of having “safe and sane”
  fireworks

  $500 for the violations involving the discharge of fireworks within the city

  enforcement response, evacuation, and related damages to the

SUBJECT:  Contract for Stage 1 Design and Engineering Services Progressive
  Design-Build Contract for the Cabrillo Mole Revitalization Project
  Phase 2

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Waive any minor irregularities in the proposal of Anderson
Burton Construction, Inc., for the Cabrillo Mole Revitalization Project Phase 2; 2. Award the
Stage I design and engineering services progressive design-build contract for the Cabrillo
Mole Revitalization Phase 2 Project to Anderson Burton Construction, Inc., thus affirming the
City Manager’s rejection on an appeal filed by Padelford; subject to finalization of such an
agreement, 3. Authorize the City Manager or designee to negotiate and bring back a contract
agreement with Anderson Burton Construction for City Council approval.

REPORT SUMMARY: Public Contract Code § 22185 et seq. authorizes the City to use
progressive design-build contracting for the Progressive Design-Build Cabrillo Mole
Revitalization Phase 2 Project (“Project”).

At a high-level, this Project includes two stages: (1) preconstruction design phase services
(“Stage 1”); and (2) final design services and construction services to complete the Project
(“Stage 2”). The selected design-builder performs the Stage 1 design and engineering services
during or after which the design-builder proposes to City a Guaranteed Maximum Price
(“GMP”) to construct the Project and, if accepted by City, the parties will enter into an
amendment to the contract for design-builder’s performance of Stage 2 services (final design
and construction). If the design is not acceptable to the City or the GMP too high, the City has
the option of not proceeding with Stage 2.

On November 17, 2025, the City of Avalon published a request for qualifications (RFQ) for the
Project. The RFQ provided qualified design-builders (“Proposers”) an opportunity to submit a
statement of qualification (“SOQ”) and demonstrate their qualifications, experience,
competence, and capacity to design and construct the replacement and expansion of the City’s
Cabrillo Mole Ferry Intermodal Terminal.

  1. Background of Request for Qualifications

The City conducted a mandatory pre-bid conference in person and virtually on December 11,
2025. The meeting included an overview of the requirements set forth in the RFQ, a walk
through the City’s design intent, as well and a site visit to the Cabrillo Mole to examine existing
 conditions and operational expectations. The original SOQ deadline was extended from
January 22 to February 5, 2026, to allow potential respondents more time to provide
comprehensive responses to the REQ.

The City received three SOQs from Proposers by the stated deadline A.J. Padelford & Sons,
  —

Inc. (“Padelford”), Anderson Burton Construction, Inc. (“Anderson”), and Benchmark
Contractors, Inc. (“Benchmark”). City Staff conducted a thorough analysis of the SOQs
received based on the evaluation criteria specified in the REQ and conducted two
meetings/interviews with each Proposer.

  2. Evaluation, Scoring, and Ranking of the Highest Ranked Proposer

The SOQs were evaluated on seven factors in accordance with California law for progressive
design-build projects, including: 1) meeting minimum pass/fail submission requirements, 2)
understanding of the project, 3) project experience and references, 4) project team and key
personnel, 5) project delivery, cost development, and management approach, 6) fee and rate
proposal for Stage 1, and 7) construction cost estimate for Stage 2. Each factor was scored
and the total scores were calculated to determine the overall ranking of the Proposers.

While City Staff made the determination that all three firms that responded to the REQ were
qualified and capable of completing the Project, Anderson was identified to be the highest
ranked Proposer based on City staff’s careful evaluation according to the seven evaluation
criteria set forth in the REQ. Anderson consistently received the highest individual scores in
each evaluation on most of the factors and was ranked highest overall among the three
Proposers. Anderson demonstrated a good understanding of the Project and developed a
detailed schedule and narrative plan illustrating how it intended to manage the Project,
including its commitment to meet the desired Project schedule, planned construction phasing,
and risk management procedures and understanding of the logistics of construction at a
remote location like Catalina Island.
